title: Why Big Tech could be a big boogeyman in 2028 | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump came into office 22 months ago previewing an alliance with Big Tech that seemedprimed to recast the future of American politics. He effectively paraded the powerful executives he had wooed to his side at his inauguration.

Now, it’s not just Trump whose fortunes have been turned decidedly upside down; Big Tech is looking like an increasingly potent political boogeyman, too.

Americans’ palpable fears about AI and distaste for data centers set the stage. And theoutages of the past weekappear likely to help solidify Big Tech’s status as a potential political punching bag ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

There isn’t yet quality polling about the recent tech outages. But the trajectory of Americans’ feelings about Big Tech has been clear for some time.

It’s headed in a decidedly negative direction.

Gallup pollingthis summer showed 8 in 10 Americans had only “some” or little-to-no confidence in large technology companies, placing them among the least-trusted institutions that were tested.

What’s more, the 41% who had little or no confidence was up from 32% last year and up from 24% in 2020.

Similarly,Fox News pollingin June showed big technology companies supplanting big government as the one registered voters viewed as the greater threat (52% to 47%, respectively). That marked a big shift from 2019, when registered voters viewed big government as the bigger threat by a substantial margin, 58%-35%.

AndCNN polling in Mayshowed 69% of Americans said they didn’t trust big technology companies like Google, Facebook and Amazon to do what’s best for their customers — a number that has continued to rise from 58% in 2019.

The poll showed the same number (69%) also didn’t trust AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta.

Those numbers come on top of all the evidence that Americans are apprehensive about what those AI companies could mean for daily life.

CNN polling this summer showed three times as many people thought AI was having anegative impact (48%) as a positive one (16%).

In addition, 75% said their prevailing emotion about AI was fear or concern rather than something positive. And 81% were “very” (45%) or “somewhat” (36%) concerned that AI would fundamentally “change our way of life.”

Polls have also long shown that Americans are much more animated by the risks of AI than its potential benefits. That’s been shown in bothWashington Post/ABC News pollingandAP/NORC polling.

A telling stat from the former poll: More Americans felt there was a “high” risk that AI would lead to human extinction (33%) than said there was a “big” chance that it would make people more productive (20%).

And a recentGallup pollshowed 27% of US workers said they were worried that technology would make their job obsolete — double where the same number stood in 2017.

The new figure is only around a quarter of those surveyed. But that’s a quarter that would seem to be extremely motivated by this issue; few things motivate voters as much as fear for their livelihood.

And that’s what’s really important here. It’s not just that people don’t like Big Tech; it’s that they’re increasingly seeing it as a threat to themselves personally. And its growing role in daily life and the economy is likely to make the issue a lot more urgent.

AI didn’t seem to play a huge role in the 2026 elections.

TheCNN Voter Pollshowed 30% of voters trusted Democrats more on AI, compared to 26% for Republicans. And only 23% of voters overall said the issue of AI and data centers was crucial to their vote — significantly less than corruption, the cost of living, the Iran war and immigration.

But that might be because the issue was so new and Americans hadn’t digested the differences between the two parties on the topic. There’s a lot more time for candidates to articulate and refine their positions ahead of 2028.

And at least one Big Tech CEO seems pretty concerned about what lies ahead for the industry politically.

Appearing at a Semafor conference Tuesday, Amazon founder Jeff Bezoscautioned against villainizing Big Tech.

“It’s a good political technique, but it’s a terrible technique for solving problems,” Bezos said.

He said the image some politicians present of Big Tech is “not a true picture. Most people in tech just want to stay heads down doing the work.”

Bezos, of course, was among the technology executives that Trump proudly invited to his inauguration. But 22 months is a long time in politics.
